title: 007/05 - CocaCola
text:
KINGDOM OF CAMBODIA 
Nation King Religion 
---------------- 
 
ARBITRATION COUNCIL 
 
Case number: 07/05 
Date of Award: 18 March 2005 
 
 
 
 
ARBITRAL AWARD 
Issued under Article 313 of the Labor Law 
 
Cambodia Beverage Company Ltd. (Coca Cola) ("CBC") 
(Employer Party) 
and 
 
Cambodian Industrial Food Union Federation ("CIFUF") and 
Worker Development Union of CBC (Coca Cola) ("WDUCBC") 
(Worker Party) 
 
DETAILS OF EMPLOYER P ARTY 
Representative: 
1- Ms. Denis Lauwens, CBC Director; 
 
 
 
2- Sar Siphin, CBC HR Manager; 
 
 
 
3- Mr. Edward Nicholas, Advisor for DFDL lawyer company; 
 
 
 
4- Ms. Mao Sam Vutheavy, lawyer. 
Address: 
#287, National Road 5, Sangkat (commune) Russey Keo, Khan (district) 
Russey Keo, Phnom Penh

(855 16) 919 415, (855 23) 428995/6

Details of Worker party 
Representative: 
1- HE Ouk Phuri, lawyer; 
 
2- Mr. Heng Bunchhun, CIFUF President; 
 
3- Mr. Nai Sok Veasna, Federal Union of Solidarity; 
 
4- Mr. Mao Keo, WDUCBC consultant; 
 
5- Mr. Un Leakhnak, worker in sales and union member; 
 
6- Mr. Nhik Kosal, floating worker; 
 
7- Mr. Bun Yan, shop steward; 
 
8- Mr. Un Sok, WDUCBC Vice President; 
 
9- Ms. Khatt Sophy, WDUCBC General Secretary; 

 
2
 
10- Mr. Duong Sok, WDUCBC financier; 
 
11- Mr. Nuon Chanthar, Dhama Thapktay Federation Union; 
 
12- Mr. Neak Heng, officer from Federal Union of Solidarity; 
 
13- Mr. Chinh Thi, CBC worker. 
Address: 
#834, National Road 5, Mittapheap village, Sangkat (commune) Russey 
Keo, Khan (district) Russey Keo, Phnom Penh. 
Telephone: 
(855 12) 868352 
 
ISSUES IN DISPUTE 
1- The worker party demands that the company reinstate Mr. Mao Keo to the production 
line, although he was transferred to another section, with duties similar to those he 
had before. The company party cannot decide on Mr. Mao Keo's case for the time 
being, pending the decision of the Labour Inspector as to whether he should be 
reinstated or dismissed. 
2- The worker party still demands that the company reinstate Mr. Un Leakhnak. The 
company party will not reinstate Mr. Un Leakhnak, thinking Mr. Un Leakhnak has 
committed serious misconduct. 
3- The worker party still demands that the company comply with the agreement dated 
23 September 2004 about floating workers, in accordance with the Labour Law. The 
company party does not respond to this demand, thinking that it has already been 
settled. 
4- The worker party still demands, based on Point 15 of the agreement, that the 
company give them wages for 21-22-23 September 2004, when workers went on 
strike. The company party will not give wages in compliance with the Labour Law. 
 
JURISDICTION OF THE ARBITRATION COUNCIL 
The Arbitration Council derives its power to make this Award from Chapter XII, Section 
2B (Articles 309-317) of the Labor Law (1997); the Prakas on the Arbitration Council 
(#099 of 21 April 2004); the Prakas on the Appointment of Arbitrators (No. 103 of 26 April 
2004 and No. 265 of 13 July 2004); and the Arbitration Council Procedural Rules which 
form an Annex to the same Prakas (No. 25 February 2005). 
 
An attempt was made to conciliate the collective dispute that is the subject of this Award, 
as required by Chapter XII, Section 2A of the Labor Law. The conciliation hearing which 
took place on 15 February 2005 was unsuccessful, and the non-conciliation report 
number 226 of 15 February 2005 was submitted to the Secretariat of the Arbitration 
Council on 25 February 2005. 

 
3
 
 
ARBITRATION PANEL 
− Arbitrator chosen by the employer party: Mr. Ouk Ry 
− Arbitrator chosen by the worker party: Mr. An Nan 
− Chair arbitrator (chosen by the two arbitrators): Mr. Kong Phallack 
 
HEARING AND SUMMARY OF PROCEDURE BEFORE THE ARBITRATION COUNCIL 
 
 
Date and place of hearing: 
First hearing: 3 March 2005 at 8:00 AM at the Secretariat of the Arbitration Council. 
Second hearing: 16 March 2005 at 8:00 at the Secretariat of the Arbitration Council. 
 
Witnesses and experts: N/A 
 
Documents, Exhibits and other evidence considered by the Arbitration Council 
A. Obtained from the employer party 
1- Brief in relation to the four issues dated 2 March 2005; 
2- Certificate of business registration dated 27 April 1998; 
3- Bylaw of the company dated 11 March 2004; 
4- Internal Work Rules of the company dated 3 October 2000; 
5- Samples of Mr. Mao Keo's and Mr. Un Leakhnak's contracts; 
6- Evidence or documents in relation to the four issues; 
7- Letter asking for a lawyer's help dated 15 March 2005. 
 
B. Obtained from the worker party 
1- Certificate of union registration dated 27 December 2004; 
2- Letter of complaint from Mr. Mao Keo dated 15 January 2005; 
3- Letter of Mr. Mao Keo's suspension dated 2 February 2005; 
4- Letter dated 20 January 2005 temporarily suspending Mrs. Mao Keo for 7 days from 21 
January 2005 to 27 January 2005; 
5- Terms of Reference of Mr. Mao Keo; 
6- Table of work assignment in the company dated 24 January 2002; 
7- Letter of complaint from Mr. Un Leakhnak dated 30 November 2004; 
8- Letter dated 8 November 2004 temporarily suspending Mr. Un Leakhnak for 7 days from 
9 November 2004 to 15 November 2004; 
9- Letter of complaint from six floating workers dated 10 January 2005; 
10- collective dispute conciliation report dated 23 September 2004; 

 
4
11- Collective dispute conciliation report dated 26 January 2005; 
12- Union's letter of complaint against CBC for violating union rights dated 15 January 2005; 
13- Union's letter dated 5 February 2005 asking to negotiate with CBC; 
14- Union's letter on deductions of wages during strike dated 28 September 2004 
15- Letter of notification of Mr. Mao Keo's dismissal dated 9 March 2005; 
16- Letter asking lawyer for help dated 13 March 2005; 
17- Letter from Attorney Uk Phuri asking to attend the hearing dated 15 March 2005; 
18- Union's letter dated 8 March 2005 in relation to CBC's allegation against Mr. Mao Keo; 
19- Letter of confirmation by Mr. Siem Sokly dated 8 March 2005; 
20- Letter on union discrimination from Mr. Un Sok and Mr. Un Sam Ol dated 8 March 2005. 
 
C. Obtained from the Ministry of Labour and Vocational Training [MoLVT] 
1- Letter of request for the resolution of a collective labour dispute at the enterprise named 
Cambodia Beverage Company (No. 245 from HE. Nhep Bunchin, MoLVT Minister) dated 
25 February 2005; 
2- Report on labour dispute resolution at CBC (No. 226 of 27 January 2005) from Mr. Huot 
Chanthy, the Head of Department of Labour Inspection; 
3- Report on collective labour dispute conciliation dated 4 February 2005. 
 
D. Provided by the Secretariat of the Arbitration Council 
1- Letter of invitation for parties to attend the hearing on 28 February 2005; 
2- Letter of invitation for parties to attend the hearing on 11 March 2005. 
 
E. Presentation and testimony of worker party and employer party 
 
F. Both parties decide at the hearing: this award will be non-binding. 
 
SUMMARY 
 
CBC is placed at #287, National Road 5, Kilometer 6 commune, Russey Keo district, Phnom 
Penh and employs 197 workers. 
 
On 24 January 2005, the Russey Keo-based Labour Inspection Office received a workers' 
phone call complaining that the company needed to improve working conditions to properly 
satisfy the Labour Law. Upon receiving the information, on 26 January 2005 the Russey Keo-
based Labour Inspection Office began the process for dispute settlement and conciliation with 

 
5
the last conciliation taking place on 4 February 2005, and two out of the six issues successfully 
conciliated; the four unsuccessfully conciliated issues, as described in the above issues, were 
referred to the Arbitration Council for resolution on 25 February 2005. 
 
On 3 March 2005 at 8:00, the Arbitration Council called upon the two parties to attend a hearing. 
At the hearing, the Arbitration Council tried to conciliate the issues further, based upon a win-win 
principle, but this failed. In regard to floating workers, the union and company agreed to allow for 
re-calculations for those workers who find that the company has not paid them enough. Also at 
the hearing, the company argued that the dismissals of Mr. Mao Keo and Mr. Un Leakhnak are 
not collective disputes, and therefore asked the Arbitration Council to consider its jurisdiction 
over those issues. 
 
On 9 March 2005, the company gave notice about Mr. Mao Keo's dismissal. Upon receiving this 
information, the Arbitration Council invited the two parties to a second hearing on 16 March 2005 
at 8:00 AM. 
 
FINDINGS OF FACT 
 
1. The first issue regarding Mao Keo's suspension. 
- Mr. Mao Keo started with the company on 31 Dec 1992. He is a union secretary and works in 
the production section, in charge of machinery operations. 
 
- Mr. Mao Keo was frequently warned for not complying with the work rules and the terms of 
reference set forth in his contract. On 6 September 2004, he was warned for the first time for 
coming to work late. On the 6
th of November 2004, he was warned for the second time, this time 
for not complying with the IWR, being late for work, and being absent without a leave form. On 
12 November 2004, the head of the production line reported to the administration department 
about Mr. Mao Keo's misconduct in not complying with the work rules and refusing to correct his 
misconduct. On 11 January 2005, Mr. Mao Keo promised to follow the terms of the contract; but 
still he refused. On 20 January 2005, the company decided to suspend him temporarily from 21 
January 2005 to 27 January 2005. On 27 January 2005, there was a meeting between the 
union and the company about Mr. Mao Keo. After the meeting, on 2 Feb 2005, the company 
decided to notify Mr. Mao Keo about the serious misconduct and suspension. Mr. Mao Keo 
received the letter on 3 Feb 2005. The company requested the Labour Inspector terminate Mr. 
Mao Keo's contract on 7 Feb 2005. On 9 March, the company notified Mr. Mao Keo about his 
dismissal, but the company agreed to put Mr. Mao Keo back on suspension [rather than 
terminate his employment] before the Arbitration Council on 16 March 05. 

 
6
- The union alleged that the Company's suspension of Mr. Mao Keo was an act of union 
discrimination, but the Company denied this. The Arbitration Council finds that the union's 
argument does not have a clear basis. 
 
- Mr. Mao Keo argued that he refused to fix machines for fear of working outside his role. The 
company stated that all this work was the previous work that Mr. Mao Keo used to do, and which 
was set out in point 6 of the terms of reference. The fact that he refused to work was because 
he was angry that the company had not increased his pay. Mr. Mao Keo insisted that the term 
had just been hand-written; however, the Arbitration Council finds that point 6 of the terms of 
reference states: "Re-assembles the welding equipment for use as spares and replace if 
required." The term that the Arbitration Council received from the two parties was not hand-
written but computer-typed. 
 
- According to the Company, Mr. Mao Keo's refusal to fix the machines caused the company's 
production line to shut down for many hours; Mr. Mao Keo did not refute the company's 
testimony. The Arbitration Council found that Mr. Mao Keo's refusal to fix the machines 
jeopardized the operations of the company. 
 
- There is only one union in the company: Union for Development of Workers of Coca Cola 
Company. The union was officially registered on 27 December 2004. 
 
2. The second issue regarding Mr. Un Leaknak's dismissal. 
- Mr. Un Leaknak started with the company on 1 Jan 1997. He is a union member while working 
in sales. 
 
- According to the employer's testimony at the hearing, the company dismissed Mr. Un Leaknak 
on 8 November 2004 for misappropriating a case of soda which was supposed to be sent to a 
customer, Chhay Sary, from the company on 28 October 2004. The company learned about the 
misappropriation of the case of soda on 7 November 2004. The company then conducted an 
investigation into this issue making inquiries to Mr. Chhay Sary who is the company's customer. 
Customer Chhay Sary told the company in a letter, dated 8 Nov 2004 that he never received the 
case that the company sent on 28 Oct 2004. 
 
- Mr. Un Leaknak did not dispute the testimony of the employer, and admitted that he had indeed 
signed for Chhay Sary but that he did not intend to take that case of soda; he just forgot to 
deliver it to Chhay Sary. 

 
7
- The union alleged that the company's suspension of Mr. Un Leaknak was an act of union 
discrimination, but the company denied this. The Arbitration Council finds that the union's 
argument did not have a clear enough basis to support the allegation. 
 
3. The third issue regarding floating workers. 
- According to the documents provided by the employer, 20 floating workers in sales and 16 in 
the production line were dismissed by the company in early January 2005. All of them had 
worked for the company for more than one year. Two workers who had worked the longest were 
worker Seng San in sales who had worked with the company for 5 years, and worker Nuon 
Phuon in the production line who had worked for the company for 6 years. In the report, the 
company did not state how many days per month or how many consecutive months each worker 
worked; it just provided a summary. In addition, the company stated that all workers were on 
undetermined duration contracts [(UDCs)] and that when the company dismissed them all they 
calculated their indemnity for dismissal as if they were regular workers. Therefore, the 
Arbitration Council finds that the company regarded those workers as regular workers. 
 
- The company dismissed all of them as it would dismiss regular workers: in compliance with 
Article 67 (7) on "non-written labour contracts", and Article 77 on "termination of contract without 
prior notice"; the company offered workers such benefits as the money regarding prior notice, 
indemnity for dismissal and annual bonuses according to the seniority of each worker. 
 
- Of the 36 workers whom the company dismissed, 6 lodged a complaint against the company in 
respect of their dismissal [arguing that it was] in violation of the Labour Law. Of the 6 workers, 3 
were in sales and the other 3 were in the production line. In the sales department were Ek Rithy, 
Im Saret, and Thinh Roatha; in the production line were Nhik Kosal, Siem Sok Ry, and Siem Sok 
Peou. The 6 workers already signed to receive their money. Five of them requested the 
company do the calculations again, while Mr. Nhik Kosal asked for reinstatement and was willing 
to give the money back to the company [if he was reinstated]. 
 
- The company agreed to do the calculation again if any worker thought the company had made 
wrong calculations and came to meet with the company, but no one has ever come to the 
company. The company agreed in the hearing to perform the calculations again if any worker 
thought that they were not right, but refused to reinstate them, not even Mr. Nhik Kosal, who 
attended the hearing. Mr. Nhik Kosal, on the other hand, insisted that the company reinstate 
him. 
 

 
8
- Five workers have not received their money yet because the company cannot find them. Four 
of them were in Sales and one in the production line. In the sales were Leng Puthy, Soeun Chan 
Voda, Sem Yuth and Nou Chitra while in the production line was Sok Rithy. 
 
- Point No. 8 of the agreement dated 23 September 2004 states, for floating workers, the 
company will do as follows, " If a worker has worked many months [and] many years and asked 
their section representative of workers to submit their name for the company to check and admit 
[him/her] as full right worker, under the Labour Law."" 
 
- The union alleged that the company's termination of the contracts of the 36 workers has 
something to do with union discrimination because the employees took an active part in the 
strike; but the company denied that there was such discrimination. The Arbitration Council finds 
that the union's contention does not have a clear enough basis to support their allegation against 
the employer. 
 
4. The fourth issue re the wage deduction for the strike of 21-22-23 September 2004 
- Workers went on strike for three days on 21-22-23 September 2004 because the company 
refused to settle with them the fact that the company had forced the sales workers to sell out 200 
cases a day. The workers recognized that there was no prior notice about the strike. The 
company argued that no new workers were recruited during the strike; the union did not object to 
the company's argument. The AC found the strike on 21-22-23 Sept 2004 did not comply with 
the legal procedures and the company did not employ new workers. 
 
- The worker party demanded the company give them wages for 21, 22 and 23 September 2004 
when all of the workers went on strike based on point 15 of the [non-conciliation] agreement. 
Point 15 of the agreement states, "Both parties, the company and worker union, agree on no 
retaliation against workers who participated in the strike. In the future, if any problem happens, 
both parties shall comply with the procedures as set forth in the Labour Law." 
 
 
REASONS FOR DECISION 
 
 
Issue over jurisdiction of the Arbitration Council 
At the hearing, the employer argued that the Arbitration Council does not have jurisdiction to 
hear the conflicts surrounding Mr. Mao Keo and Mr. Un Leaknak because they are individual 
disputes and not collective ones. Before deciding whether or not it has jurisdiction over the 
issues, the Arbitration Council will explain whether these are individual or collective disputes. 

 
9
According to Section 12 of Chapter II of the Labour Law, the Arbitration Council does not have 
jurisdiction to hear an individual dispute but it finds that the Labour Inspector and the Minister in 
charge of Labour have a duty to decide whether a dispute is individual or collective before 
sending it to the Arbitration Council . Therefore, the Arbitration Council will follow the decision of 
the Labour Inspector and the Minister in charge of Labour unless there are clear reasons not to. 
(Please read Case 41/04-Mikasa, Case 02/04-Cambodiana, and Case 10/03-Jacqsintex) 
 
In this case, the Arbitration Council also agrees with the decision by the Minister in charge of 
Labour that the disputes are collective because they satisfy the three conditions of a collective 
dispute, as is set out in Article 302 of the Labour Law. The conditions are: 
a- a dispute between a number of workers and one or more employers; 
b- an issue in relation to work conditions, the exercise of the rights given to a professional 
organisation, the recognition of a professional organization or an issue regarding the 
relationship between employer and workers; 
c- this issue can jeopardize the effective operation of the factory. 
 
In this case, conditions a - c are satisfied so the disputes are collective. Condition A is satisfied 
because the issue was brought up by the union, which represents the workers. A union is an 
organization which represents a group of workers (see Article 266 of the Labour Law). 
Therefore, the condition that a collective dispute must concern a group of workers is satisfied as 
the union brought the complaint. Condition B is satisfied because the disputes involve an issue 
about whether or not workers are being dismissed for their union activities and the exercise of 
the rights given to the professional organization (the right to carry out union activities without 
interference from the employer). Moreover, the dismissals of Mr. Mao Keo and Mr. Un 
Leakhnak are issues regarding the employment relationship. Condition C is satisfied because 
the disputes could put the company's operation at risk, because workers may go on strike or 
take other industrial action about this issue. Therefore the Arbitration Council agrees with the 
decision of the Ministry of Labour and the head of the Labor Inspection Department who decided 
that the disputes regarding Mr. Mao Keo and Mr. Un Leaknak are collective disputes (please see 
91/04-Honeywear). Accordingly, the Arbitration Council has jurisdiction to resolve the issues 
regarding Mr. Mao Keo and Mr. Un Leaknak. 
 
The first issue regarding Mr. Mao Keo's suspension: 
In this case, the employer mentioned that (s)he decided to suspend Mr. Mao Keo in accordance 
with Art. 295, which provides, in the case of serious misconduct, the manager of enterprise can 
render the decision to instantly suspend the party in question pending the Labour Inspector's 

 
10
decision. If the Labour Inspector turns down the dismissal, the suspension is annulled and its 
effects are cancelled lawfully. 
 
According to this Article, the employer can suspend Mr. Mao Keo's contract only in cases of 
serious misconduct, as is stipulated in Art. 83(B). Art. 83(B) of the 1997 Labour Law which 
states, "The following are considered to be serious offences: 
1- stealing, misappropriation, embezzlement. 
2- Fraudulent acts committed at the time of signing (presentation of false documentation) or 
during employment, sabotage, refusal to comply with the terms of the employment 
contract, divulging professional confidentiality. 
3- serious infractions of disciplinary, safety and health regulations. 
4- threat, abusive language or assault against the employer or the workers. 
5- inciting other workers to commit serious offences. 
6- political propaganda, activities or demonstrations in the establishment. 
 
According to the employer's claim in the hearing, Mr. Mao Keo's misconduct consists of a refusal 
to comply with the terms of his employment contract, as is stated in point 2 of Art. 83(B). 
 
According to the findings of fact by the Arbitration Council, Mr. Mao Keo was wrong indeed as he 
refused to comply with the terms of the employment contract. Even Mr. Mao Keo himself 
admitted that he had refused to work at the order of his superior although it was the work he had 
done before. A mere refusal to work at the order of the superior cannot be regarded as serious 
misconduct, especially if the refusal does not shut down the operation of the enterprise; 
however, the company claimed that in the case of Mr. Mao Keo it did jeopardize the whole 
production. Mr. Mao Keo's refusal to work did shut down the production for many hours. Mr. 
Mao Keo did not object when the company brought this issue up. Under the circumstances of 
this case, after Mr. Mao Keo learnt that the company would not raise his wages, he refused to fix 
the machines. Mr. Mao Keo should have known that his refusal to repair the machines would 
seriously shut down the operations of the company. Such conduct is comparable to sabotage. 
Under Article 83(B)(2), sabotage can be serious misconduct. 
 
In response to the company's argument above, Mr. Mao Keo and the union argued that the 
dismissal of Mr. Mao Keo concerns union discrimination. The company argued that there was 
no union discrimination. In this case, the Arbitration Council finds that the union's allegation of 
discrimination is not based on sufficient evidence. 
 

 
11
In conclusion, in consideration of the particular facts of this case, the Arbitration Council finds 
that Mr. Mao Keo did commit serious misconduct and the employer complied properly with the 
procedures of the Labour Law because both Mr. Mao Keo and the union did not show any 
evidence against the employer's presentation. Therefore, the Arbitration Council rejects the 
workers' claim for Mr. Mao Keo's reinstatement. 
 
The second issue regarding Mr. Un Leaknak's dismissal: 
Just as Mr. Mao Keo's case, the company dismissed Mr. Un Leaknak for committing serious 
misconduct, as stipulated in Art. 83(B) of the 1997 Labour Law. 
 
According to the employer's claim at the hearing, Mr. Un Leaknak's misconduct included 
stealing, misappropriation and embezzlement as is set forth in 83(B)(1). According to the 
findings of fact by the Arbitration Council, Mr. Un Leaknak did indeed commit serious misconduct 
as he admitted taking a case of soda on 28 October 2004 after the company learned of the issue 
on 7 November 2004. 
 
Art. 26 [of the Labour Law] states, in pertinent part, "The employer shall be considered to 
renounce his right to dismiss a worker for serious misconduct if this action is not taken within a 
period of seven days from the date on which he/she has learned about the serious misconduct in 
question." 
 
In this case, the employer took action to dismiss Mr. Un Leaknak on 8 November 2004. 
Therefore, because the Arbitration Council finds that Mr. Un Leaknak committed an act of 
serious misconduct and the employer acted to dismiss him within a period of seven days from 
the date on which the employer learned about the serious misconduct, the Arbitration Council 
rejects the workers' demand that the employer reinstate Mr. Un Leaknak. 
 
The third issue regarding the floating workers. 
Art. 9 of the Labour Law states that casual workers (called floating workers by the company) are 
individuals who enter into a contract to perform a specific task that must normally be completed 
within a short period of time, or who performs work occasionally, intermittently and seasonally. In 
previous awards, the Arbitration Council has decided that floating workers in garment factories 
who work 21 days for two consecutive months shall be converted to regular workers. Art. 166 (3) 
of the Labour Law, regarding annual leave, states that for the jobs that are not performed 
regularly throughout the year, a worker in an enterprise works 21 days per month on average, 
then they shall be regarded as regular. 

 
12
The Arbitration Council found out that each floating worker at CBC has worked at least one year 
according to the company's total report, although the report does not state that each worker has 
worked 21 days per month on average of two consecutive months. In addition, the company 
also recognized all the workers as regular workers of the company because the company 
dismissed them in accordance with the procedures that apply to regular workers. 
 
According to the above interpretation, these floating workers (1)- are not casual workers, as is 
defined in the Art. 9, and (2)- are regular workers, as is set forth in Art. 166 and Art 9. 
 
Thus, the employer had already regarded these workers as regular workers, as set forth in Point 
8 of the agreement on 23 September 2004 regarding casual workers; the company party agrees 
as follows: "If a worker has worked many months [and] many years and asked their section 
representative of workers to submit their name for the company to check and admit [him/her] as 
full right worker, under the Labour Law." However, since the existence of the agreement, the 
company has never admitted these workers as regular workers; but terminated the contracts of 
those floating workers with wages. 
At the hearing, the company did not give clear reasons why it refused to admit those workers as 
regular workers; the company just said that (1) the company could not afford to reinstate them; 
(2) the company already paid those workers according to the Labour Law Art. 67(7) and Article 
77 as though it dismissed regular workers; (3) the company has already allowed a local 
company to provide their labour force instead and the company has already notified the workers 
of this. 
 
In this case, 36 workers were dismissed; almost all of them received an indemnity for their 
dismissal. Six of the 36 workers brought a complaint through the union, one of whom, Mr. Nhik 
Kosal, demanded reinstatement and the other five demanding re-calculation. The company only 
agreed to the five workers' demand that the company re-calculate the money, but not to the 
demand of Mr. Nhik Kosal that the company reinstate him as a regular worker and in return he 
offered to return the money he received to the company; the company disagreed. 
 
Therefore, based on the above facts and interpretation, the Arbitration Council will determine 
whether or not the dismissal of the six workers described above whose contracts were UDCs 
was legally proper. 
 
Besides serious misconduct, the company can also terminate labour contracts of workers in 
accordance with the following: 

 
13
a. In case of operational requirements of the company 
In this case, the Arbitration Council determines that the company did not provide any evidence to 
show there were any operational requirements of the company. 
 
b. Based on Labour Law provisions 
A termination of a UDC must comply with the following Articles: Article 116 regarding payment 
of wages; Articles 75 and 77 regarding prior Notice; Article 89 regarding dismissal indemnity; 
Article 91 regarding damages; Article 166, and 167 regarding annual leave. 
 
In this case, the Arbitration Council determines that the company did not include benefits (only 
wages) in the calculation of (1) compensation for Notice (2) dismissal indemnity. As for the 
dismissal indemnity, it was not properly calculated according to Article 168 of the Labour Law. 
 
c. Termination of contract in accordance with Points a and b, above, may be executed 
unless it goes against the Labour Law 
[See] Article 12 regarding no discrimination; Article 279 regarding protection for union freedom; 
and Article 74 regarding dismissal for invalid reasons. 
 
In this case, the Arbitration Council determines that the union's claim that there was 
discrimination was not sufficiently established to increase the burden to the employer. The 
company on the other hand, did not provide any evidence regarding the requirements of the 
company's operation. Article 91(1) of the Labour Law provides " The termination of a labor 
contract without valid reason by either party to the contract entitles the other party to damages." 
However, in this case, the employer did not have clear reasons in accordance with Article 91(2) 
of the Labour Law; "These damages are not the same as compensation in lieu of prior notice or 
the dismissal indemnity." Therefore, the workers whose contracts were terminated by the 
employer are entitled to damages. According to Article 91(3), "The workers can request to be 
given a lump sum equal to the dismissal indemnity, in which case (s)he is relieved of the 
obligation to provide proof of damage incurred." 
 
For the case of Mr. Nhik Kosal who wished to return to work, the company should consider 
giving him a chance to return to work. If the employer does not agree, Mr. Nhik Kosal is entitled 
to damages just as other workers are. 
 
In conclusion, the Company did not calculate the money for the 36 workers properly. For this 
reason, all the workers have the right to demand the Company perform re-calculations. 

 
14
The fourth issue regarding the deduction of wages for going on strike on 21, 22, 23 
September 2004. 
 
Article 332 of the Labour Law states that a strike suspends the labour contract. During a strike, 
allowances for work are not provided and the salary is not paid. The worker shall be reinstated 
in his job at the end of the strike. 
 
However, Article 334 states that during a strike, the employer is prohibited from recruiting new 
workers as replacements for the strikers except in order to maintain minimum services as 
provided in Articles 326 and 328 if the workers who are required to provide such service do not 
appear for work. Any violation of this rule obligates the employer to pay the salaries of the 
striking workers for the duration of the strike. 
 
The Arbitration Council decided in case 04/03-Lida Garment, protection of employees who took 
part in a strike according to Article 334 may be fully applied only if the workers went on strike in 
compliance with the procedures set forth in the Labour Law. Thus, in order to decide whether or 
not the strikers are entitled to wages during the strike, the Arbitration Council will consider as 
follows: 
 
- Did the employer party recruit new workers to replace the strikers during the strike? 
- Was the strike carried out in accordance with the procedures set forth in the law? 
 
1. Did the employer party recruit new workers for a replacement for the strikers during 
the strike? 
 
In the hearing the employer party said that they did not recruit new workers during the strike 
because during that time the factory was completely closed without any workers being able to 
work. As for the workers, they also agreed that there had been no recruitment of new workers. 
This shows that the company really did not recruit new workers. 
 
2. Are the workers entitled to wages and bonuses during the strike? 
 
Under Article 324 of the LL, before going on strike, workers must give notice at least seven 
working days in advance. But the workers did not give prior notice; they started their strike right 
away because the company forced the workers in sales to sell 200 cases of soda per day and 
the employer refused to negotiate with the workers. 

 
15
Similarly, Article 333 of the Labour Law prohibits the employer from imposing punishment in any 
form against strikers. The prohibition is fully effective unless the strike was not organized in 
accordance with the strike procedures. If workers do not follow the law, they may not be fully 
entitled to the benefits of protection under the law. 
 
However, in the non-conciliation report of the Ministry, the worker party demanded the company 
give them wages for 21, 22, 23 September 2004 when all the workers went on strike on the 
basis of point 15 of the agreement. Point 15 of the agreement states, "Both parties, the 
company and worker union, agree on no retaliation against workers who participated in the 
strike. In the future, if any problem happens, both parties shall comply with the procedures as is 
set forth in the Labour Law." 
 
The Arbitration Council finds that the intended meaning of this agreement does not provide for 
no deduction of wages but for no retaliation and compliance with the Labour Law. In the hearing, 
the employer said that they complied with the agreement and with the Labour Law and did not 
retaliate against any worker; all workers were allowed to return to work. However, the workers 
thought that the deduction was retaliation. An agreement is a contract. Article 1 of the Decree-
Law No. 38 of 1988 states that, a contract is an agreed will between two or more individuals in 
order to create, modify or abolish one or more obligations involving themselves. In this case, the 
agreement made between the workers and the employer is unclear because the word 
"retaliation" in the agreement fails to clarify what it means. Article 23 of the Decree-Law No. 38 
of 1988 states that, where a contract is made with unclear meaning, such a contract shall be 
interpreted based on practice or customs of the place where the contract is made as long as 
such an interpretation is not against the provisions of this Decree-Law. In case of doubt, such a 
contract shall be interpreted in favor of the debtor party. 
 
In this case, the Arbitration Council finds that the company is the debtor party to the agreement 
of 23 September 2004. 
 
In conclusion, the Arbitration Council finds that the deduction of wages is not retaliation because 
the Labour Law does not provide clearly for the issue of not giving wages during a strike. 
Therefore, the company's refusal to give wages during the strike is proper. (Please read case 
04/03-Lida Garment; case 08/04-Washcompanyncept; case 15/04-Lucky Zone; case 16/04-
Yada Printing; case 25/04-Standard Garment; case 47/04-Dai Young; case 111/04-Sunshiny; 
and case 03/05-Flying Dragon) 
 

 
16
Based on the foregoing facts, evidence and law, the Arbitration Council decides in this Award as 
follows: 
 
DECISION 
1. Reject the workers' demand for the employer to reinstate Mr. Mao Keo. 
2. Reject the wokers' demand for the employer to reinstate Mr. Un Leaknak. 
3. Order the employer to compensate floating workers equally in respect of layoff 
compensation if any of them makes the demand. Order the employer to do the 
calculation again for any worker who demands that the calculation of compensation led 
to underpayment. The employer must cooperate with union representatives to resolve 
this issue as from the date this Award takes effect. 
4. Reject the demand of workers for the company to pay wages for 21-22-23 September 
2004 when workers went on strike.
